subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: fMRI measures brain activity by detecting changes in:
options: Blood oxygenation and flow (the haemodynamic response)
questions.explain: fMRI detects the haemodynamic response, measuring changes in blood-oxygen levels and flow associated with neural activity.

questions.q: Locus of control, as a concept relevant to resisting social influence, was proposed by whom?
questions.explain: Julian Rotter proposed the concept of locus of control, distinguishing internal from external control.

questions.q: In Loftus and Palmer's second experiment, participants who heard 'smashed' were more likely to report what a week later?
options: Seeing broken glass that was not present
questions.explain: The 'smashed' group falsely recalled seeing broken glass, showing leading questions can alter the memory itself.

questions.q: Which of the following is a methodological weakness of using animal studies (Lorenz, Harlow) to explain human attachment?
options: Findings may not generalise from animals to humans due to differences in cognition and behaviour
They cannot establish cause and effect
questions.explain: A key limitation is reduced generalisability, as humans differ from geese and monkeys in cognitive and emotional complexity.

questions.q: In the working memory model, the phonological loop deals with which type of information?
questions.explain: The phonological loop processes auditory and speech-based (verbal) information.

questions.q: Which process transfers information from STM to LTM in the multi-store model?
questions.explain: Rehearsal in the rehearsal loop transfers material from STM into LTM in the multi-store model.

questions.q: Axonal sprouting, a mechanism of functional recovery, involves:
options: The growth of new nerve endings to connect with undamaged neurons
The thickening of the myelin sheath
questions.explain: Axonal sprouting is the growth of new nerve endings that reconnect neurons whose links were damaged, aiding recovery.

questions.q: In Asch's study, conformity dropped sharply when one confederate gave the correct answer. This shows the effect of what?
questions.explain: A dissenting confederate broke the group's unanimity, providing social support and reducing conformity dramatically.

questions.q: A strength of Schaffer and Emerson's study is that observations were made in:
options: A controlled laboratory using the Strange Situation
The infants' own homes by parents, giving high ecological validity
questions.explain: Data were gathered in the family home through parental reports, giving the findings high ecological validity.

questions.q: In Bowlby's 44 Thieves study, affectionless psychopathy was most associated with:
options: Early and prolonged separation from the mother
questions.explain: Bowlby found the affectionless thieves were far more likely to have experienced early prolonged maternal separation.

questions.q: On a typical neuron, the structures that receive signals from neighbouring neurons are the:
questions.explain: Dendrites receive incoming signals and carry electrical impulses towards the cell body of the neuron.

questions.q: Which study is most associated with demonstrating destructive obedience?
questions.explain: Milgram's 1963 study is the classic demonstration of obedience to a destructive authority figure.

questions.q: What was the approximate average conformity rate to incorrect answers in Asch's baseline study?
questions.explain: Participants conformed to the wrong majority answer on about one-third (33%) of the critical trials.

questions.q: Knowledge of facts, concepts and the meaning of words is stored in which memory type?
questions.explain: Semantic memory holds shared general knowledge of facts, concepts and meanings.

questions.q: An excitatory neurotransmitter such as adrenaline acting on a postsynaptic neuron will:
questions.explain: Excitatory neurotransmitters make the postsynaptic neuron more positively charged, increasing the likelihood of an action potential.

questions.q: Which component of working memory handles visual and spatial information?
questions.explain: The visuo-spatial sketchpad stores and manipulates visual and spatial data.

questions.q: According to research, what is the duration of the short-term memory store?
questions.explain: STM has a limited duration of roughly 18-30 seconds without rehearsal, as shown by Peterson and Peterson.

questions.q: Which type of neuron carries messages from the central nervous system to effectors such as muscles?
questions.explain: Motor neurons carry signals from the CNS to effectors (muscles and glands) to produce a response.

questions.q: In Asch's variations, what happened to conformity when the task was made more difficult?
questions.explain: Greater task difficulty increases ambiguity, raising informational social influence and therefore conformity.

questions.q: During synaptic transmission, neurotransmitters are released from the presynaptic neuron and cross the:
questions.explain: Neurotransmitters diffuse across the synaptic cleft (gap) to bind with receptors on the postsynaptic neuron.

questions.q: Interference is most likely to cause forgetting when the two sets of information are what?
questions.explain: Interference effects are strongest when the competing memories are similar, as McGeoch and McDonald showed.

questions.q: Moscovici's blue-green slide study primarily investigated which process?
questions.explain: Moscovici examined how a consistent minority could influence a majority's judgements of slide colour.

questions.q: In Bowlby's theory, what is meant by 'monotropy'?
options: A learned association between caregiver and food
A special, primary attachment to one particular caregiver
The tendency to imprint on the first moving object
questions.explain: Monotropy refers to the infant's single, primary attachment to one main figure, which Bowlby saw as the most important.

questions.q: Publicly agreeing with a group to gain approval while privately disagreeing is best described as which type of conformity?
questions.explain: Compliance is a superficial, temporary public change without private acceptance of the group's view.

questions.q: Proactive interference occurs when what happens?
options: New information disrupts recall of older information
Information decays in the sensory register
Older information disrupts recall of newer information
questions.explain: In proactive interference, previously learned information disrupts the recall of more recently learned information.

questions.q: In Ainsworth's Strange Situation, what is the procedure primarily designed to measure?
options: The strength of the internal working model directly
The quality or type of attachment
questions.explain: The Strange Situation is a controlled observation designed to assess the type or quality of an infant's attachment.

questions.q: Who developed the working memory model?
questions.explain: The working memory model was proposed by Baddeley and Hitch in 1974.

questions.q: Recalling information best when in the same physical environment as when it was learned is an example of what?
questions.explain: Context-dependent retrieval shows recall improves when external cues at retrieval match those at encoding (e.g. Godden and Baddeley's divers).

questions.q: Broca's area, associated with speech production, is typically located in the:
questions.explain: Broca's area lies in the left frontal lobe and damage to it causes difficulty in producing fluent speech.

questions.q: The cognitive interview was developed by Fisher and Geiselman to do what?
options: Improve the accuracy and amount of recall from eyewitnesses
questions.explain: The cognitive interview uses psychological techniques to enhance the quantity and accuracy of eyewitness recall.
